One raster, many maps

The same pixels, filtered to one question at a time. Each of these is a find or an area away.

At full resolution

The overview above is decimated 7× to fit on a screen. At 0.50 m/px the actual raster resolves individual buildings and vehicles — these crops are untouched pixels.

S5 Natural-language querying

Six verbs that answer quantitative questions in code, so no model ever does arithmetic over a big table.

Why it earns its place. In-context arithmetic over a large table is exactly where LLMs go wrong, and exactly what is easy to compute. The verbs are not the user interface — they are the tool surface a model is given, and having them exist first is what keeps the model out of the numbers.

The algorithm

  1. describe — Class histogram over classified pixels, with region counts and the nodata fraction stated.
  2. count / area / find — Filterable by minarea, slope, near. count counts connected components, so two houses sharing a wall are one — the tool description says so.
  3. distance — True pixel-to-pixel closest approach between two classes, returning both endpoints so it can be checked on the map.
  4. corridor — Threshold the S4 trafficability raster, remove passages narrower than the vehicle, connected-component the result, and report which components touch the seed class.
  5. Carry the evidence — Every result carries the region / component ids it was computed from. An answer without ids cannot be audited.
Where it abstains. A slope filter with no DEM is unanswerable, not '0 degrees'. A class outside the vocabulary is unanswerable with the reason — vehicle type, building function, fences, anything about colour.

The two refusals above are the point. count Truck and a slope filter with no DEM both return unanswerable with a reason. Neither returns zero. A silent plausible answer to an unanswerable question is the failure mode this whole surface exists to prevent.

Does count count the right thing?

count counts connected components, so two houses sharing a wall are one house and a row of parked cars is one car. The tool description says so — which is not the same as being right. Measured on this raster:

classcomponentstotal m² median m²largest m²largest shareimplied by area
House8169,5242344,82964%~1,159components are fused
Car242,5588728811%~213components are fused
BrickWall121,705141,32978%—no reference size — not assessed

On this map, no. the largest House component is 44,829 m² and holds 64% of all House area, with a median component of 23 m² where a house is about 60 m²; the largest Car component is 288 m² and holds 11% of all Car area, with a median component of 87 m² where a car is about 12 m². Those are not individual objects — they are everything that touches, fused into one component. A count over them is a count of blobs, and the honest reading of the area column is ~1,159 House; ~213 Car by area, not the component count.

This is S5's open question 9, answered empirically rather than asserted. It is a property of this segmentation, not of the verb — run segmap showcase on your own raster and the table is recomputed for it. The fix is instance segmentation or a watershed split, neither of which is in this repo.

Run it on your own map. 
segmap solve s5 --query '...' -i data/incoming/sinai/tile_cropped_x801_y846_z0.5.tif --query "count House minarea 40"

Or open the Solutions tab of segmap ui -i <your-raster.tif> and press Run S5. If your GeoTIFF has no ID_TO_LABEL_MAPPING tag, add --classes your_class_ids.json.

S4 Derived decision products

The many-to-one mapping from 47 classes + slope + season into what someone actually asks for.

Why it earns its place. A model helps at authoring time — hand-writing 47×N lookup tables with exceptions is tedious and error-prone. But once authored the tables are checked in and evaluation is fully deterministic. No LLM in the runtime path.

The algorithm

  1. Look up a per-class base score — One number per class per product, from a checked-in table.
  2. Apply the modifiers — Vehicle type (wheeled / tracked / foot) and season (wet / dry) shift the scores — a clay soil that carries a wheeled vehicle in August does not in February.
  3. Penalise by slope and roughness — Where a DEM exists. Without one this step is skipped and the product is a class lookup only.
  4. Emit a 0..1 raster — Plus a summary by superclass, so the shape of the answer is legible before anyone opens the image.
Where it abstains. With no DEM the slope penalty never applies, so every figure here is a surface-type score and not a real trafficability estimate. The corridor verb in S5 inherits exactly this.

Where the two meet: corridor

The most interesting verb, because it is S5 riding on S4 and it inherits every guess S4 makes. It answers "where can a wheeled vehicle actually get to from the road network" with no model involved at all.

# corridor (wheeled, seeded from DirtRoad): corridor DirtRoad vehicle wheeled
# 97.3% of the classified area is reachable from DirtRoad without leaving ground passable to a wheeled vehicle (threshold 0.45, slope limit 25.0 deg, passages narrower than the vehicle width 2.5 m (5 px opening) removed); 3 reachable pocket(s) totalling 152 m2 below 500 m2 excluded as noise from the table and the headline figure
= 16,086,883.54
component	area_m2	tile_frac	cy	cx
1	16086884	97.3%	4124	4118
# evidence: component ids 1
Read the assumptions, not the number. The note states all three: the trafficability threshold, the slope limit, and the vehicle width used to close narrow passages. Every one of them is a guess inherited from S4, and with no DEM the slope limit never actually binds.

S1 Consistency audit

Flag labels that contradict their own context, slope or geometry, then roll thousands of flags up into the handful of distinct facts they are instances of.

Why it earns its place. It is the only solution whose output feeds back into the segmenter: a confirmed finding becomes a training-data correction, and the flag rate per class is an error map you get without any detection ground truth.

The algorithm

  1. Index every region — Connected components per class, each with area, perimeter, compactness, elongation, and a neighbour graph carrying the shared boundary length with every touching region.
  2. Run five check families — context-prior (does this class sit next to what it should?), slope-prior and aspect-prior (does the morphology match?), lithology-isolation (a limestone unit with no carbonate neighbour is suspect), and nari-geometry. Each emits a finding with a severity graded from the evidence, not a fixed constant.
  3. Roll up to root causes — Findings sharing a class-level fact are one decision for a reviewer, not N. 2710 findings collapse into 62 causes, each naming example region ids.
  4. Rank by review value — severity × area0.5 — so a systematic fact over a large area outranks one loud speck.
  5. Report coverage first — Which classes had an active check at all. A class with no check is unexamined, not clean, and the report refuses to let zero findings imply otherwise.
Where it abstains. With no DEM every slope and aspect is 0.0 — a valid-looking number meaning unmeasured. The slope and aspect priors do not run rather than score against a fabricated zero.

S2 Confusion adjudication

S1 says region 245 is wrong. S2 answers then what is it? — and refuses when the evidence cannot separate the candidates.

Why it earns its place. Limestone / Dolomite / Nari rocky terrain are not separable in RGB even for a human expert. A system that confidently picks one is manufacturing corruptions. UNDECIDABLE-NEEDS-geological-map is a first-class verdict, and it is designed to fire often.

The algorithm

  1. Build a candidate list — The incumbent label plus the classes it is plausibly confused with — same lithology, adjacent rung on an ordinal series, or common neighbours.
  2. Score three evidence terms — context — what fraction of this region's boundary is shared with units of the same lithology; morphology — slope and aspect against the class prior; geometry — compactness and elongation against what the class looks like.
  3. Require a margin — A challenger must beat the incumbent by 0.15 to earn a SWITCH. Inside the margin the verdict is KEEP or UNDECIDABLE — never a coin flip presented as a finding.
  4. Show the whole table — Every candidate with its three sub-scores and the note explaining each, so the verdict can be disagreed with.
Where it abstains. Without a DEM the morphology term is unscored for every candidate, which is stated in each row rather than silently scored 0.5.

S3 Cost-aware detection triage

Use the cheap segmentation as a prior to decide which image chips are worth sending to an expensive detector.

Why it earns its place. This is the solution with a direct cost line. The model is not in the per-chip loop — it compiles a query into a small cacheable policy once, and a deterministic scorer applies it to millions of chips. An LLM call per chip replaces one expensive call with another and saves nothing.

The algorithm

  1. Compile the query into a policy — Once per query type: class weights, a hard-exclude list, and a regime. Cacheable, checked in, human-readable.
  2. Score every chip — Pure arithmetic over the precomputed chip index — class fractions, entropy, edge density, distance to anchor classes. Milliseconds over millions of chips.
  3. Hard-exclude the impossible — Vehicles cannot park on boulder fields, steep smooth rock, dissected badlands, or water. Those chips cost nothing to skip.
  4. Spend the budget top-down — Take the highest-scoring chips until the budget fraction is used.
  5. Sample a control set — A mandatory random sample of the rejected chips. Without it there is no unbiased recall signal and the triage can never be shown to be wrong.
Where it abstains. 'Score captured' is prior mass, not recall. The report says so in capitals: real recall needs detector outcomes that do not exist yet.

All three policies, on this map's 1,024 chips

segmap solve s3 --policy vehicles|structures|oov -i data/incoming/sinai/tile_cropped_x801_y846_z0.5.tif --policy vehicles --budget-frac 0.02

Or open the Solutions tab of segmap ui -i <your-raster.tif> and press Run S3. If your GeoTIFF has no ID_TO_LABEL_MAPPING tag, add --classes your_class_ids.json.

S6 Change reasoning

Classify each transition between two dates, because the same raw pixel difference means completely different things.

Why it earns its place. A pixel diff of two label maps is mostly noise and phenology. GreenGrassland → DryGrassland means the season changed and the ground did not; Batha → House means someone built something. Only one of those is worth a phone call.

The algorithm

  1. Diff co-valid pixels only — A pixel that is nodata on either date is not a change.
  2. Classify every transition — Into phenology, succession, construction, impossible, and so on — from the taxonomy's own structure, the degradation and road series.
  3. Guard the implausible — A multi-stage jump along a succession series in one season is a classifier disagreement, not regrowth.
  4. Component-count each pair — So '400 scattered pixels' and 'one new building' are told apart.
Where it abstains. An impossible transition is reported as evidence about the classifier, not about the ground — and every one of them is free ground truth for S1.
Not demonstrated on this map. S6 needs two rasters of the same footprint at different dates, and there is only one date here. Everything above is what it would do; nothing below it is a result.

The transition classes it sorts into

transitioncategorywhat it means
GreenGrassland → DryGrasslandphenologythe season changed, the ground did not
Batha → Gariguesuccessionregrowth, or a boundary wobble
DryGrassland → Houseconstructionsomeone built something — the one worth a phone call
Water → LimestoneBoulderimpossibleevidence about the classifier, not the ground; free ground truth for S1
Run it on your own map. 
segmap solve s6 --second t2.tif -i data/incoming/sinai/tile_cropped_x801_y846_z0.5.tif --second <second-date.tif>

Or open the Solutions tab of segmap ui -i <your-raster.tif> and press Run S6. If your GeoTIFF has no ID_TO_LABEL_MAPPING tag, add --classes your_class_ids.json.

Run all of this on your own map

Nothing on this page is specific to the tile it was built from. Point any of it at your own raster and every image, table and number is recomputed from yours.

1 — the interactive demo

segmap ui -i /path/to/your-raster.tif
# -> http://127.0.0.1:8765

Three tabs. Verbs runs the S5 query language by hand; Solutions runs S1–S6 with their options; Ask is the one path that needs an Anthropic API key. The other two never call a model.

2 — regenerate this page for your map

segmap showcase -i /path/to/your-raster.tif -o out/showcase.html

3 — one solution at a time

segmap solve s1 -i your.tif                      # audit
segmap solve s2 -i your.tif --region 1817        # adjudicate one region
segmap solve s3 -i your.tif --policy vehicles    # triage
segmap solve s4 -i your.tif --product concealment
segmap solve s5 -i your.tif --query "count House minarea 40"
segmap solve s6 -i your.tif --second date2.tif   # change

What your raster needs

thingrequired?notes
Single-band label rasteryesGeoTIFF, .npy or single-band PNG. Class ids, not a colourised RGB export.
Class id → name mappingyesRead automatically from an ID_TO_LABEL_MAPPING GeoTIFF tag; otherwise pass --classes ids.json.
Metres per pixelyesTaken from the GeoTIFF transform, or pass --gsd. Every area, count threshold and distance depends on it.
A DEMno, but--dem. Without it slope and aspect are unmeasured, S1's morphology priors do not run, S2 cannot score morphology, S4 skips the slope penalty and S5 refuses slope filters. It is the single biggest upgrade available.
A second dateno--second. Required for S6 and nothing else.
An API keynoOnly for segmap ask. All six solutions are deterministic and run offline.

Big rasters: the index build is the only slow step and it is cached in .segmap_cache/, so the first command on a new tile pays it and every later one loads in seconds. To poke at a huge AOI without waiting, add --max-mpx 40 — it crops to a centred window and says so in every answer.

Generated by segmap showcase. Every image, table and number on this page was computed from the raster named at the top — none of it is illustrative. Nothing here called a language model: all six solutions are deterministic.
